Sixteen topics in COVID-19 education research: whole abstracts as a hypergraph

honets

2026-09-06

The covid corpus bundled with sbert: abstracts of COVID-19 research on education, children, schools and society, 2020 to 2024, each with its publication year. Here every abstract is one node of a document-word hypergraph and is read whole. No sentence encoder is involved, so nothing is truncated at a token window. Every number and figure is recomputed at knit time.

The corpus

Records indexed without an abstract are dropped, as are exact duplicate abstracts. Bare numbers never enter the vocabulary (the tokeniser keeps alphabetic tokens only), so the year and “19” need no stop list; the scientific boilerplate that every abstract shares does, because a word in every document separates nothing.

# clean_text() repairs the export: HTML, references, URLs, the trailing
# copyright notice (a publisher cluster at any fine cut if left in) and the
# database's placeholder for a missing abstract; unique() collapses
# duplicated records
abstracts <- clean_text(sbert::covid, column = "Abstract",
                        remove = "no abstract available", min_content = 0.5)
abstracts <- unique(abstracts)
abstracts$doc <- sprintf("abs_%04d", seq_len(nrow(abstracts)))
table(abstracts$Year)

2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 
 644 2373  542  106    5 
boilerplate <- c("covid", "coronavirus", "sars", "cov", "pandemic",
                 "disease", "study", "studies", "result", "results",
                 "conclusion", "conclusions", "background", "method",
                 "methods", "objective", "aim")

The hypergraph

Documents are nodes; every word kept after the stop lists that occurs in at least five abstracts is a hyperedge binding the abstracts that use it, with tf-idf incidence weights, stored sparse.

hg <- text_hypergraph(abstracts, column = "Abstract", id = "doc",
                      weight = "tfidf",
                      stop_words = c(stop_words_en(), boilerplate),
                      min_count = 5L, sparse = TRUE)
hg
Text hypergraph: 3666 documents, 6232 words (documents as nodes, weight = tfidf)
Hyperedges: 6232 (words); sizes 1-2595, median 14

Sixteen topics, and what the spectrum says about that

The count used throughout is sixteen, the number of topics in the published structural topic model of this literature (Saqr et al. 2023, Universal Access in the Information Society), so the partition is the one a reader of that paper can set beside its topics. The Laplacian spectrum should be read alongside that choice rather than hidden by it: the gap after the second eigenvalue is the large one, the gaps after the third and fourth are an order of magnitude smaller, and from the fifth on there is nothing. Two and four are the cuts the hypergraph itself insists on; sixteen is a finer partition below those seams, supported by the words each topic owns (next section) rather than by the spectrum.

Heavy words and distinctive words

hg_keywords() ranks each topic’s words under the score named in type. Ranked by the score itself, every topic in this corpus returns the same list: “education”, “students”, “learning”, “online”, “teaching” are the corpus, not the topics. Class-based tf-idf demotes them only mildly, because BERTopic’s idf term is log(A / f + 1) and these words are frequent in every class.

sort_by = "share" ranks by the fraction of a word’s total score that falls in the topic, and min_docs is the support floor that keeps a word owned by a topic because it occurs in a handful of abstracts from reaching the top. This is where the sixteen topics separate.

distinctive <- hg_keywords(hg, topics, n = 8, type = "frequency",
                           sort_by = "share", min_docs = 15)
knitr::kable(
  hg_keywords(hg, topics, n = 8, type = "frequency",
              sort_by = "share", min_docs = 15, collapse = TRUE),
  row.names = FALSE
)

Four views side by side

The same sixteen topics under frequency, class-based tf-idf, PageRank centrality in the topic’s own word hypergraph (words as nodes, the topic’s abstracts as hyperedges, tf-idf weights) and, when torch is present, HyperGAT attention, all ranked by share with the same support floor, so the columns differ only in how the words are scored.

views <- hg_keywords(hg, topics, n = 6, sort_by = "share", min_docs = 15,
                     centrality = "pagerank",
                     type = c("frequency", "ctfidf", "centrality"))
plot(views, value = "share")

attention <- hg_hypergat(abstracts, labels = topics, column = "Abstract",
                         id = "doc", epochs = 10, seed = 1,
                         what = "attention")
fit <- hg_hypergat(abstracts, labels = topics, column = "Abstract", id = "doc",
                   epochs = 10, seed = 1)
mean(fit$predicted == fit$label)
[1] 0.9683579

Topics across the pandemic years

Each abstract carries its publication year, so the partition doubles as a lens on how the literature moved. Sixteen topics cannot be told apart by colour, so each topic gets its own panel: the bar is the topic’s share of that year’s abstracts, labelled by the three words the topic owns most. 2023 holds 105 abstracts and should be read with that in mind; 2024, with five, is left to the count table.

labels <- hg_keywords(hg, topics, n = 3, type = "frequency",
                      sort_by = "share", min_docs = 15, collapse = TRUE)
year_topic <- merge(topics, subset(abstracts, select = c(doc, Year)),
                    by.x = "node", by.y = "doc")
year_n <- as.data.frame(table(Year = year_topic$Year))
shown <- subset(merge(year_topic, year_n, by = "Year"), Freq >= 30)
composition <- as.data.frame(
  prop.table(table(shown$Year, shown$cluster), margin = 1)
)
names(composition) <- c("year", "cluster", "share")
composition <- merge(composition, labels, by = "cluster")
composition$topic <- factor(composition$words, levels = labels$words)
composition$label <- sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * composition$share)
ggplot2::ggplot(composition,
                ggplot2::aes(x = .data$year, y = .data$share)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = okabe_ito[5], width = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = .data$label), vjust = -0.4,
                     size = 3) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(.data$topic), ncol = 3) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x),
                              expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, .3))) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "publication year", y = "share of the year's abstracts") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 9))

knitr::kable(
  as.data.frame.matrix(table(year_topic$Year, year_topic$cluster)),
  caption = "Abstracts per year and topic"
)

Document scope against sentence scope, at sixteen topics

The centrality view above relates two words when they share an abstract. text_hypergraph(construction = "sentence") builds the finer relation: words are nodes and every sentence is a hyperedge, so two words are linked only when they share a sentence. Passed to hg_keywords() in place of the document hypergraph, with the same partition, it ranks each topic’s words by their centrality among the topic’s sentences rather than its abstracts. The comparison uses the same sixteen topics as the rest of the document.

sh <- text_hypergraph(abstracts, column = "Abstract", id = "doc",
                      construction = "sentence",
                      stop_words = c(stop_words_en(), boilerplate),
                      min_count = 5L, sparse = TRUE)
sh

Hyperedges: 30637 (sentences); sizes 1-74, median 12

[1] 7.625

The two scopes share seven or eight of eight words in every one of the sixteen topics. Ranked by share, a topic’s owned vocabulary is what surfaces under either scope, and centrality only orders it; the finer co-occurrence relation changes that order at the margin. Sentence scope does not remove the corpus vocabulary either: ranked by raw centrality instead of share, “learning”, “students”, “education” and “online” top every topic under both scopes, because the words of the whole corpus are also the words of most sentences.

The scope matters more, and in the other direction, for word communities. Cutting the document-scoped word hypergraph (nodes = "word") into sixteen gives communities of a few hundred words each; cutting the sentence-scoped one gives two large communities and fourteen small ones, the usual spectral behaviour on a sparse relation.

word_bag <- text_hypergraph(abstracts, column = "Abstract", id = "doc",
                            nodes = "word",
                            stop_words = c(stop_words_en(), boilerplate),
                            min_count = 5L, sparse = TRUE)
communities <- lapply(list(document = word_bag, sentence = sh), \(h) {
  parts <- hg_cluster(h, k = 16, seed = 1)
  degree <- Matrix::rowSums(h$incidence)
  sizes <- sort(table(parts$cluster), decreasing = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    community = names(sizes),
    n_words = as.integer(sizes),
    top_words = vapply(names(sizes), \(cl) {
      w <- parts$node[parts$cluster == cl]
      paste(utils::head(w[order(-degree[w])], 6), collapse = ", ")
    }, character(1))
  )
})
knitr::kable(communities$document, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Word communities, document scope (words as nodes, abstracts as hyperedges)")

So for this corpus the sentence construction is the better relation but not the better tool: it sharpens the ordering within a topic’s owned words slightly and it fragments word communities. Where it should pay off is a corpus whose documents are long and mixed, where sharing a document means little and sharing a sentence means a lot.

Reading it

Ranked by the raw score, the sixteen topics look alike because the corpus has one vocabulary; ranked by share with a support floor they are sixteen different literatures, under document and sentence scope alike. The three views agree on what each topic owns, since the share column is computed from the same partition; they differ in which owned word comes first. The attention view, when torch is present, is trained on these same four labels, and its agreement with them is printed above its table. The year composition is descriptive: it reports shares, not a test of change over time.
